messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is a 41-year-old South Asian man who works as a park ranger in a large state forest in the Pacific Northwest. He has been in a committed relationship for six years and, until recently, was regarded by his colleagues as one of the most capable and self-sufficient rangers on the team. He presented for therapy following what he described as a gradual but unmistakable deterioration in his ability to function at work and at home, and he came with the quiet, careful manner of someone who had spent a long time deciding whether to come at all.

Approximately three years ago, Rajan was taken captive by a small armed group while conducting a solo survey in a remote section of the park that bordered federally contested land. The men were dressed in military-style tactical gear and carried weapons. They detained him for several days in a makeshift structure, during which he was physically restrained, subjected to interrogation about park access routes and surveillance schedules, and at several points beaten. He described one particular moment — being forced to kneel on a concrete floor while a man in a tactical vest stood directly over him, speaking slowly and deliberately — as the image that returns most often. It sits in his mind not as a continuous scene but as a series of frozen frames: the shadow on the wall, the pattern of the vest, the specific angle of the man's face. When those images return, Rajan reports feeling the pressure in his knees and a sharp ache across his ribs as vividly as he felt them then, as though his body has retained its own record of the event independently of his will. At other times the same memories surface and he feels nothing at all — he can recount what happened in a flat, detached voice, as if reading a case file about someone he has never met.

In the months after his release, Rajan returned to work earlier than his supervisors recommended. He told himself this was resilience. What he did not tell anyone was that he had begun scanning the tree line every time he heard movement in his peripheral vision, and that when a colleague approached him quickly from the side one afternoon, he spun and grabbed the man's arm before he had any conscious thought. He was deeply ashamed of this. He had come to believe, with a certainty he could not argue himself out of, that the world remained actively dangerous regardless of what anyone told him — his partner's reassurances, his supervisor's assurances that the individuals responsible had been apprehended, none of it settled into him as real. Safety felt like a story other people told.

Conversations that drifted toward military topics — veterans' policy, armed conflict, even a colleague mentioning a relative who served — produced an abrupt internal contraction Rajan could not fully explain. He began redirecting such conversations, then avoiding the colleagues who raised them. When visitors to the park wore camouflage or ranger-adjacent uniforms, he found reasons to assign their interactions to other staff. He had also begun eating in a way that he understood, on some level, was about control: measuring portions, refusing to eat in groups, maintaining a strict regimen that gave him the sensation of governing at least one domain of his life precisely. In group settings, he found himself agreeing with whatever was proposed, accommodating requests he would previously have declined, telling himself that compliance was simply easier — that friction of any kind felt like a risk he could not afford.

What Rajan found hardest to articulate, and what surfaced slowly across the first sessions, was a profound sense of humiliation that he carried as a permanent feature of himself rather than a response to what had happened. He was certain that another man — someone more capable, more alert, more competent — would not have been in that situation. This belief had quietly reshaped how he moved through his days, keeping him slightly apart from his colleagues, slightly outside his own relationship, as though he no longer fully belonged to the life he had built.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work when a new ranger, young and eager, asked him directly for advice about solo fieldwork in remote terrain. Rajan opened his mouth and found he had nothing to say. He drove home that evening and told his partner, for the first time, that something was wrong. What he hoped for, he said haltingly, was to feel like himself again. What he feared most was that there was no longer a self to return to.
